title: Longest Valid Parentheses: stack tracking indices.
shortTitle: Longest Valid Parentheses: Stack Tracking Indices
keyPoints: Use a stack of indices seeded with -1 as a base marker to track the boundary of valid runs.
On '(' push its index; on ')' pop, then if empty push current index as new base, else measure length as i minus new top.
The base marker always holds the index of the most recent position that broke validity.
Time is O(n) with a single scan; space is O(n) for the stack.
A constant-space alternative scans left-to-right and right-to-left with open/close counters.
Pop before measuring is essential: it reveals the enclosing boundary and avoids off-by-one errors.

s1_definition.oneliner: Push indices with a base marker of -1, and on each closer pop and measure the valid run length back to the new stack top.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Longest Valid Parentheses** – finds the length of the longest contiguous substring of round brackets that is correctly balanced.
- **Index stack** – stores indices rather than characters, seeded with -1 as a base marker representing the position just before the string.
- **On '('** – push the index onto the stack.
- **On ')'** – pop the top, then if the stack is empty push the current index as a new base, otherwise compute the length as the current index minus the new stack top.
- **Base marker** – the bottom of the stack always holds the most recent position that broke validity, enabling correct length calculation.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time with one scan and O(n) space for the stack.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a long string of grouping markers from a partially corrupted fee formula and wants to find the longest unbroken balanced stretch for salvage parsing. Think of keeping a stack of positions. When you open a bracket, you note its position. When you close one, you pair it off and measure how long the balanced run now extends from here back to the last broken position. The widest such run is the answer.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Index Stack Walk for ")()())"
  ─────────────────────────────

  Init: stack = [-1]

  i=0 ')': pop -1 → stack empty → push 0 as new base
  stack = [0]

  i=1 '(': push 1
  stack = [1, 0]

  i=2 ')': pop 1 → stack = [0] → len = 2 - 0 = 2, max=2

  i=3 '(': push 3
  stack = [3, 0]

  i=4 ')': pop 3 → stack = [0] → len = 4 - 0 = 4, max=4

  i=5 ')': pop 0 → stack empty → push 5 as new base
  stack = [5]

  Answer: 4
```

```text
  Base Marker Concept
  ────────────────────
  String:  )  (  )  (  )  )
  Index:   0  1  2  3  4  5
           ▲              ▲
           │              │
        base 1         base 2
     (unmatched ')') (unmatched ')')

  Valid run "()()" spans indices 1..4
  Length = 4 - base1_index = 4 - 0 = 4
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Valid Parentheses finds the length of the longest contiguous balanced substring, and unlike a simple validity check it needs positions, so I use a stack of indices seeded with a -1 base marker. For every `(` I push its index. For every `)` I pop, then if the stack is empty this closer is unmatched and becomes a new base that I push, otherwise the valid run length is the current index minus the new stack top, which I use to update the maximum.

The base marker is the heart of the method. The bottom of the stack always holds the index of the most recent position that broke validity, either the initial -1 or an unmatched closing bracket. Subtracting it from the current index captures the full length of the valid substring ending here, including runs that span several adjacent or nested pairs. That is why the stack stores indices rather than bracket characters.

The subtle correctness point is that I must pop before measuring. When I meet a closer, popping removes the matched opener's index and the new top becomes the boundary of the enclosing valid run, so the subtraction spans every inner completed pair. Measuring before popping would produce an off-by-one error, which is a classic bug in this problem. I also know the constant-space two-pass counter variant, scanning left to right and right to left and resetting when one count exceeds the other, which I offer when memory is tight.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this on grouping-marker strings from partially corrupted fee-formula fragments to recover the longest intact balanced section for salvage parsing. The base marker resets correctly at each broken section, so the system finds the maximum usable portion of the formula rather than discarding the entire string.

Remember one sentence: seed the index stack with -1, pop before measuring, and the valid run length is always the current index minus the new stack top.
